Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝑿i)+ϵi,f(𝒙)=0.5x1+sin⁡(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝒙0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝒙0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.

I use seed 20250 for this question. The true mean response is f(𝒙0)=0.5(0.5)+sin⁡(0.7)−0.3(1)2≈0.5942f(\mathbf x_0)=0.5(0.5)+\sin(0.7)-0.3(1)^2\approx0.5942.

Show the workflow 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

np.random.seed(20250)
n = 400
p = 3
k_values = np.arange(1, 30, 2)
x0 = np.array([[0.5, 0.7, 1]])
f0 = 0.5 * x0[0, 0] + np.sin(x0[0, 1]) - 0.3 * x0[0, 2] ** 2
print("f(x0) =", round(f0, 6))

X = np.random.normal(size=(n, p))
y = 0.5 * X[:, 0] + np.sin(X[:, 1]) - 0.3 * X[:, 2] ** 2 + np.random.normal(0, 0.1, n)

pred_one = np.zeros(len(k_values))
for m, k in enumerate(k_values):
    knn_fit = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=int(k), weights="uniform", algorithm="brute")
    knn_fit.fit(X, y)
    pred_one[m] = knn_fit.predict(x0)[0]

print(pd.DataFrame({"k": k_values, "prediction": pred_one}).round(4).to_string(index=False))

The predictions bounce around the true value 0.59420.5942 for every kk, but any single dataset only gives one noisy estimate per kk; we need repeated datasets to separate bias from variance.

  1. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

Show the workflow 
nsim = 200
pred = np.full((nsim, len(k_values)), np.nan)
for l in range(nsim):
    X = np.random.normal(size=(n, p))
    y = 0.5 * X[:, 0] + np.sin(X[:, 1]) - 0.3 * X[:, 2] ** 2 + np.random.normal(0, 0.1, n)
    for m, k in enumerate(k_values):
        knn_fit = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=int(k), weights="uniform", algorithm="brute")
        knn_fit.fit(X, y)
        pred[l, m] = knn_fit.predict(x0)[0]

bias = pred.mean(axis=0) - f0
variance = pred.var(axis=0, ddof=0)
mse = ((pred - f0) ** 2).mean(axis=0)
print(pd.DataFrame({"k": k_values, "bias": bias, "variance": variance, "MSE": mse}).round(5).to_string(index=False))
print("Largest |MSE - bias^2 - variance| =", np.max(np.abs(mse - bias ** 2 - variance)))

Show the workflow 
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.5))
plt.plot(k_values, bias ** 2, "o-", label="Squared bias")
plt.plot(k_values, variance, "o-", label="Variance")

The decomposition holds up to rounding error (∼10−16\sim10^{-16}). As kk grows, variance falls sharply (each prediction averages more responses) while squared bias rises steadily (the neighborhood reaches points farther from 𝒙0\mathbf x_0, whose mean response differs more from f(𝒙0)f(\mathbf x_0)). MSE is U-shaped, bottoming out around k≈7k\approx7-1313.

This mirrors the ridge/lasso trade-off: more penalty there, like more kk here, trades variance for bias by making the fit less flexible. The mechanisms differ — ridge/lasso shrink coefficients, KNN changes which observations get averaged. Also, since both training locations and responses change across repetitions here, the variance reflects sampling variability in the neighborhood itself, not just the conditional noise 0.12/k0.1^2/k that would apply with fixed neighbor locations.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ‖𝜷‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝑿∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.

I use seed 20251.

Show the workflow 
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

np.random.seed(20251)
n = 400
p = 30
lambda_grid = np.logspace(0, -4, 41)
results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Setting": ["Independent", "Correlated"],
    "KNN_MSE": np.nan, "Lasso_MSE": np.nan,
    "Lambda": np.nan, "Nonzero": 0
})

for l in range(2):
    Sigma = np.eye(p)
    if l == 1:
        Sigma = 0.8 + 0.2 * np.eye(p)

    X = np.random.normal(size=(n + 1000, p)) @ np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma).T
    y = (0.5 * X[:, 0] + np.sin(X[:, 1]) - 0.3 * X[:, 2] ** 2
         + np.random.normal(scale=0.1, size=n + 1000))
    test_X, test_y = X[n:, :], y[n:]
    X, y = X[:n, :], y[:n]

    knn_fit = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=5, weights="uniform", algorithm="brute")
    knn_fit.fit(X, y)
    results.loc[l, "KNN_MSE"] = np.mean((test_y - knn_fit.predict(test_X)) ** 2)

    # Estimate means and scales separately within each training fold.
    fold = np.random.permutation(np.repeat(np.arange(10), n // 10))
    cv_mse = np.zeros((10, len(lambda_grid)))
    for m in range(10):
        X_mean = X[fold != m, :].mean(axis=0)
        X_sd = X[fold != m, :].std(axis=0, ddof=0)
        X_fit = (X[fold != m, :] - X_mean) / X_sd
        X_valid = (X[fold == m, :] - X_mean) / X_sd
        y_mean = y[fold != m].mean()
        for h, lam in enumerate(lambda_grid):
            lasso_fit = Lasso(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-8, max_iter=100000)
            lasso_fit.fit(X_fit, y[fold != m] - y_mean)
            y_hat = lasso_fit.predict(X_valid) + y_mean
            cv_mse[m, h] = np.mean((y[fold == m] - y_hat) ** 2)
    lambda_min = lambda_grid[np.argmin(cv_mse.mean(axis=0))]

    # Refit on all training observations and keep these transformations for the test set.
    X_mean = X.mean(axis=0)
    X_sd = X.std(axis=0, ddof=0)
    X_fit = (X - X_mean) / X_sd
    test_X_fit = (test_X - X_mean) / X_sd
    y_mean = y.mean()
    lasso_fit = Lasso(alpha=lambda_min, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-8, max_iter=100000)
    lasso_fit.fit(X_fit, y - y_mean)
    test_pred = lasso_fit.predict(test_X_fit) + y_mean

    results.loc[l, "Lasso_MSE"] = np.mean((test_y - test_pred) ** 2)
    results.loc[l, "Lambda"] = lambda_min
    results.loc[l, "Nonzero"] = np.count_nonzero(lasso_fit.coef_)

print(results.round(4).to_string(index=False))
    Setting  KNN_MSE  Lasso_MSE  Lambda  Nonzero
Independent   0.6124     0.3390  0.0398        5
 Correlated   0.1680     0.2142  0.0200        8
  1. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

In this run, lasso has the smaller test MSE with independent covariates (0.3390.339 vs. 0.6120.612 for KNN), while KNN has the smaller test MSE with correlated covariates (0.1680.168 vs. 0.2140.214 for lasso). With independent covariates, 27 of the 30 dimensions are pure noise, so Euclidean distance is dominated by directions irrelevant to YY, and 5NN’s neighbors need not be close in X1,X2,X3X_1,X_2,X_3. With Σjl=0.8\Sigma_{jl}=0.8, the covariates move together, so Euclidean closeness is also informative about the relevant coordinates, which helps KNN. Lasso fits a separate coefficient per covariate and can zero most out (only 5 and 8 nonzero here), so it is far less sensitive to irrelevant coordinates than a neighborhood search is.

  1. The response model contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

Lasso can only fit a linear combination, so it cannot represent sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) or −0.3X32-0.3X_3^2; its intercept absorbs only their average level, not how they vary across observations. This is a structural disadvantage unrelated to correlation, and would remain even with the correct nonlinear terms. With one dataset per setting, this only shows what happened in these particular realizations — it does not establish that correlation always helps KNN or that either method is universally better; the outcome depends on the regression function, the correlation structure, and how well each model’s assumptions fit the data.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i+𝜼i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝑨∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝒁i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝜼i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝑨\mathbf A. Generate 𝑨\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝑿\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝒁\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.

I use seed 20253.

  1. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

The m=3m=3 curve has lower average test MSE at every kk shown, and both curves are lowest around k=10k=10-1818. Even though only two latent variables enter YY, distance is computed on all 100 covariates, which are driven by all mm latent directions plus noise. When m=3m=3, the 100-dimensional signal has limited underlying structure, so most informative variation is tied to the same few directions that matter for YY. When m=30m=30, distance also responds to many latent directions unrelated to YY; two points can be close in the two relevant coordinates yet far apart in the other 28, making Euclidean neighbors less reliable.

The noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i perturbs every observed coordinate independently. Without it, 𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i\mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i would lie exactly in the column space of 𝑨\mathbf A, a subspace of dimension at most mm; with noise added, 𝑿i\mathbf X_i is scattered around that subspace instead. So this is a lower-dimensional signal buried in 100-dimensional noisy measurements, not literally mm-dimensional data, and the extra latent directions at m=30m=30 still degrade Euclidean neighborhoods even though the response mechanism is unchanged.

Question 4: Classify handwritten digits

Use zip.train and zip.test from the R package ElemStatLearn, as in the lecture. Each image has 16×16=25616\times16=256 pixel values. The first column is the digit label and the remaining columns are the pixel values. Use the first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test. Use the original pixel values without standardization, and do not include the digit label in a distance calculation.

For a test image 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 and a training image 𝒙i\mathbf x_i, the two distances are

dE(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256(x0j−xij)2,dM(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256|x0j−xij|. d_E(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{256}(x_{0j}-x_{ij})^2}, \qquad d_M(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sum_{j=1}^{256}|x_{0j}-x_{ij}|.

  1. Write a 5NN classification function that allows either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. For each test image, calculate its distances to the training images directly, find the five nearest, and return the most frequent digit label. Break distance ties by the smaller training row number and voting ties by the smallest digit. Do not use a built-in distance or KNN function for this part.

This question has no random component, so no seed is needed.

Show the workflow 
zip_train = np.loadtxt("data/knn/zip-train.csv.gz", delimiter=",")
zip_test = np.loadtxt("data/knn/zip-test.csv.gz", delimiter=",")

def euclidean_distance(x0, X):
    return np.sqrt(np.sum((X - x0) ** 2, axis=1))

def manhattan_distance(x0, X):
    return np.sum(np.abs(X - x0), axis=1)

X = zip_train[:1000, 1:]
y = zip_train[:1000, 0].astype(int)
X_test = zip_test[:500, 1:]
y_test = zip_test[:500, 0].astype(int)

def knn_classify(X, y, X_test, distance):
    y_hat = np.zeros(X_test.shape[0], dtype=int)
    for i in range(X_test.shape[0]):
        d = distance(X_test[i], X)
        # np.argsort is stable, so ties in distance break by the smaller row
        # number; np.argmax on np.bincount breaks vote ties by the smallest digit.
        neighbors = np.argsort(d, kind="stable")[:5]
        y_hat[i] = np.argmax(np.bincount(y[neighbors], minlength=10))
    return y_hat

y_hat = np.column_stack((knn_classify(X, y, X_test, euclidean_distance),
                          knn_classify(X, y, X_test, manhattan_distance)))
print("classifier built")
classifier built

    plt.subplot(1, 3, l + 1)
    plt.imshow(zip_test[i, 1:].reshape(16, 16), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest")
    plt.title(f"True: {y_test[i]}  Predicted: {y_hat[i, 0]}")
    plt.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("Different predictions:", np.sum(y_hat[:, 0] != y_hat[:, 1]))
print(pd.crosstab(pd.Series(y_hat[:, 0] == y_test, name="Euclidean correct"),
                  pd.Series(y_hat[:, 1] == y_test, name="Manhattan correct")))
Different predictions: 22
Manhattan correct  False  True 
Euclidean correct              
False                 58      3
True                  11    428

These are test rows 4, 13, and 14 (1-indexed), with true labels 6, 2, and 4 misread as 0, 0, and 7. The “6” has an unusually rounded, closed lower loop, the “2” has a heavily curved outline, and the “4” is missing a clear horizontal crossbar — all plausible reasons a pixel-distance rule would confuse them, even though a person can still recognize most of them.

The two distances agree on 478 of 500 predictions but disagree on 22: Euclidean is correct while Manhattan is wrong on 11 of those, the reverse on 3, and on the remaining 8 both are wrong but predict different digits. So yes — a similar overall error rate (0.1220.122 vs. 0.1380.138) can hide disagreement on which specific images each rule gets wrong.

Question 5: Create a plot-formatting skill

  1. Include a title, a description, and a few formatting rules. The description should limit the skill to STAT 432 homework plot improvements and require an explicit request to use it. Your rules should address margins, titles, axes, labels, colors, and sizes for plots produced in R or Python. Keep them portable: do not refer to specific homework questions.

I wrote and installed the skill at .claude/skills/format-homework-plots/SKILL.md in the repository root, alongside the existing explain-to-me skill. Its content is:

---
name: format-homework-plots
description: Use only when the user explicitly calls this skill to improve the formatting of a STAT 432 homework plot.
metadata:
  version: "1.0.0"
---

# format-homework-plots

## Intent

Improve the visual formatting of a plot from a STAT 432 homework, in R or
Python, without changing the underlying data, calculations, or statistical
content. Only run when I explicitly ask for this skill by name on a
specific plot.

## Rules

- Preserve the plotted data, calculations, and statistical meaning exactly.
  Never change what is plotted, only how it looks.
- Leave enough margin so titles, axis labels, tick labels, and legends are
  never clipped or overlapping.
- Give the plot a short, informative title that states what is shown.
- Label both axes clearly, including units when relevant, and use tick
  spacing/labels that are easy to read at the chosen figure size.
- Use a colorblind-friendly, high-contrast palette; when curves could be
  confused by color alone, also vary line style or marker shape.
- Default to a 6.5 by 4.5 inch figure, 12-point axis/tick labels, and a
  14-point title, and place the legend where it does not cover the data;
  widen the figure or shrink font sizes proportionally for multi-panel
  figures.
- Apply these rules directly to the existing R or Python plotting code for
  the named plot; do not rewrite the analysis code around it.

## Out of scope

Do not use this skill on plots I have not named, and do not use it to
change results, recompute statistics, or restyle any part of the homework
other than the requested plot.
  1. Ask your agent to install the skill. Explicitly call it to improve the plot from Question 1, then compare the original and revised versions. Do you like the changes? You may revise the skill and test it a couple more times, or uninstall it if it remains unhelpful.

I asked: “Use format-homework-plots to improve the formatting of my Question 1 plot.” The skill reused the exact bias, variance, and mse arrays computed above (no data or calculations changed) and produced a version with a title, axis labels, larger fonts, a colorblind-friendly palette, and distinct markers per curve:

Show the workflow 
plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
plt.plot(k_values, bias ** 2, "o-", color="#0072B2", label="Squared bias")
plt.plot(k_values, variance, "s-", color="#E69F00", label="Variance")
plt.plot(k_values, mse, "^-", color="#009E73", label="MSE")
plt.xlabel("Number of neighbors k", fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel("Squared error", fontsize=12)
plt.title("Bias-variance decomposition of KNN at " r"$\mathbf{x}_0$", fontsize=14)
plt.xticks(k_values[::2], fontsize=10)
plt.yticks(fontsize=10)
plt.ylim(bottom=0)
plt.legend(fontsize=11, loc="upper right", frameon=True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Compared with the original, the revised version adds a descriptive title, explicit axis labels, larger fonts, a colorblind-friendly palette, and distinct marker shapes as a second cue beyond color. I like these changes and kept the skill as written — the original was fine for quick inspection while working, but the revised one reads better without the surrounding text. No revision to the skill was needed after this test.

  1. Append your final SKILL.md content to your submission and briefly explain your choices and experience.

My final SKILL.md is the one shown in part a — unchanged after testing. I limited the description to an explicit-request trigger so it never fires unintentionally while I’m working on other parts of the homework, and I wrote the rules to touch only presentation (titles, labels, fonts, colors, margins, sizes), explicitly forbidding changes to the underlying data or computation. Keeping the rules free of question-specific references is what let the same skill apply unchanged to the Question 1 plot, and should work equally well on any other plot in this or a future homework.
